On the night of Ramchandra Ray's escape, Udayaditya is the commanding, decisive figure who forcefully kicks the locked door, orders Sitaram to open it, draws his sword, and—at the deferential guard's request—disarms and binds him before orchestrating the escape, while Sitaram submits helplessly out of gratitude to the prince who had saved his life twice. On the night of Udayaditya's own escape from prison, these roles completely reverse: Sitaram takes charge as the decisive rescuer who throws open the prison door, urgently grabs and nearly carries Udayaditya outside, and commands him to follow, while Udayaditya is passive and disoriented after his long confinement, helplessly asking Sitaram what he should do and where he should go.

Pratapaditya's initial, failed plan was to have two Pathan brothers assassinate Basanta Ray on his way to Jessore—specifically ordering them to kill him when he took shelter at the inn in Simultali. In carrying this out on the road, one brother lured Basanta Ray's retainers away by falsely wailing that dacoits had attacked a village, leaving the other brother to kill the unprotected king, but the plan failed when the Pathan could not bring himself to do it and confessed the plot instead.

The method that finally succeeds is an explicit written death sentence signed by Pratapaditya and executed by Muktiyar Khan and his soldiers. After capturing Udayaditya outside the palace, Muktiyar Khan and his men shed their military uniforms, concealed their weapons, and infiltrated the Raigarh fort in plain clothes through different gates in the evening. They surrounded Basanta Ray's room and presented Pratapaditya's signed order; after Basanta Ray submitted and prostrated himself in prayer, Muktiyar Khan summoned Abdul, who entered the room and killed Basanta Ray with a sword.

1. In the Mahishi's room in the inner quarters of the palace in Jessore, where he is disguised as a middle-aged woman.
2. In a room in King Ramchandra Ray's palace in Chandradwip, where he is not wearing any disguise and appears simply as himself, the jester.

When the Rajmahishi sends Matangini to secretly fetch medicine from Mangala (Rukmini) to win back Udayaditya's heart, Mangala instead prepares a poison accompanied by mantras and rituals, which results in Surma's death the night before her scheduled exile.

Feeling deeply insulted and seeking revenge for her refusal, her husband, King Ramchandra Ray, decides to take another wife. Consequently, when Vibha later arrives in Chandradwip, she discovers that the king is getting married that very day and offers her no forgiveness, leaving her with no place in her own kingdom or royal palace and shattering all her hopes of happiness.

Rukmini obtains the ring—which has a seal engraved with the Yubaraj's name—from Udayaditya when he gives it to her in desperation to keep her from sitting on his bed. Sitaram and Bhagavat then use the ring to stamp a forged petition addressed to the Emperor, making it appear as though Udayaditya is accusing Pratapaditya of treason in order to claim the kingdom for himself. Instead of taking the document to Delhi as planned, Bhagavat delivers the stamped petition to Pratapaditya, claiming he obtained it after intercepting a servant of Udayaditya who was carrying it to Delhi and subsequently fled. Upon seeing the forged petition, Pratapaditya flies into a rage and orders Udayaditya's imprisonment; even though Pratapaditya admits to his minister that he does not particularly believe Udayaditya actually did it, he uses the petition as grounds to keep him imprisoned under guard so that he cannot do anything in secret.

To help Ramchandra Ray escape at midnight, Udayaditya overpowered and bound the palace guards to open the locked doors. As a repercussion, Pratapaditya dismissed the two guards, Sitaram and Bhagavat, from their jobs and began paying close attention to Udayaditya. Feeling guilty for causing their dismissal and Sitaram's resulting poverty, Udayaditya arranged a monthly stipend for both men. When Pratapaditya learned of this, he became enraged and forbade Udayaditya or anyone else from providing them financial help. To protect Udayaditya while still aiding the guards' starving families, Surma took over the responsibility and secretly sent stipends to Sitaram's mother and Bhagavat's wife through a maid. Because the maid did not keep this secret from Mangala, word of the secret stipends eventually reached Pratapaditya, prompting him to issue an order sending Surma away to her paternal home.

The song "I alone am left behind" signifies Basanta Ray’s profound loneliness, sorrow, and sense of emptiness, reflecting his grief that the loved ones he once embraced and sang for are gone, leaving him without joy or the spirit to go on living by himself.

He sings it in two contrasting contexts: first, in quiet, wistful solitude from afar while sitting on the veranda of his palace in Raigarh gazing at the setting sun—before knowing of Udayaditya’s imprisonment—as he longs for his loved ones in Jessore and wonders if he will ever see them again (and briefly echoes it somberly when Khan Saheb asks to hear him sing); second, in direct confrontation with stark reality inside the royal palace in Jessore after learning of Udayaditya’s imprisonment, as he holds a weeping Vibha’s hand before Surma’s dark, silent, and utterly empty room, realizing that the joyful household that once greeted him is truly gone.

After failing to stop the escape and surviving her jump into the canal, Rukmini goes to Pratapaditya's court and exposes Sitaram's staged prison fire, revealing that Udayaditya is alive and fled with Basanta Ray. She requests men to track them down, and after those men confirm that Udayaditya is in Raigarh—where Rukmini remains—Pratapaditya dispatches his Pathan commander, Muktiyar Khan, with a secret signed order sentencing Basanta Ray to death. In Raigarh, Rukmini leads Muktiyar Khan and his soldiers directly to Udayaditya in a grove outside the palace so they can capture him, after which Muktiyar Khan and his men infiltrate the fort in plain clothes, present Pratapaditya's death warrant to Basanta Ray, and have a soldier named Abdul kill him with a sword.

Pratapaditya’s initial reception of Ramchandra Ray is marked by calm, aloof indifference and effortless face-to-face superiority, whereas Ramchandra later addresses Pratapaditya’s status through obsessive, daily, behind-the-back ridicule in his own court. When Ramchandra visits Jessore, Pratapaditya refuses to concern himself with welcoming arrangements, greets his son-in-law without any joy or haste, focuses on state business while reading documents, interrupts Ramchandra mid-sentence, and casually dismisses him to the inner quarters—leaving Ramchandra bowed, subdued, and acutely aware of Pratapaditya’s superiority. In contrast, once back in his own court, Ramchandra relies on loud flattery and mockery to assert dominance over an absent Pratapaditya: he puts a poor subject on trial simply for discussing the incident between them, allows no court session to adjourn until his courtiers have aimed verbal attacks at Pratapaditya’s back, and smokes his hookah with immense, smiling pleasure as his minister, Dewan, and jester demean Pratapaditya’s brief royal lineage, belittle his family's status, and tear an imaginary figure of him to shreds.

Rukmini leaves Raigarh, changes her name to Mangala, and settles on the outskirts of Jessore, where she befriends the palace servants to track every piece of news from the palace in hopes of one day ruling over Udayaditya's heart and kingdom. When the Rajmahishi hears of Mangala's knowledge of tantra, mantra, and medicine and sends Matangini to secretly fetch medicine to turn Udayaditya's heart away from Surma, Rukmini instead spends five days preparing a poison—along with mantras and rituals intended to make Udayaditya feel no pity—which leads to Surma's death by poisoning. Following Surma's death, Rukmini directly confronts Udayaditya by entering his darkened bedchamber during a storm in soiled, torn clothes, weeping and blaming him for ruining her, demanding his love, and leaving with the ring from his finger after he stops her from sitting on his bed.

Udayaditya's early wish not to be the crown prince and his conviction that he is unfit to rule culminate in a formal renunciation after he is brought before Pratapaditya as a prisoner from Raigarh following his grand-uncle's murder. Overwhelmed by despair over his weakness and revulsion toward his father, Udayaditya agrees when Pratapaditya declares him unworthy of the kingdom and pleads to be granted release from the throne. When Pratapaditya questions his sincerity, Udayaditya states that Samaraditya will be the heir and requests only to be allowed to leave for Kashi with money to establish a guest house and a temple in his grand-uncle's name. After Pratapaditya agrees, Udayaditya goes to the temple that very day and, in front of his father, touches the feet of Ma-Kali to formally swear an oath that as long as he lives, he will not accept even an iota of the kingdom of Jessore, sit on its throne, or touch its royal scepter—declaring that if he ever does, all the sin of his grand-uncle's murder will be his.

Fearing what Pratapaditya might do if he received the letter, the messenger Nayanchand decides to deliver it to the Mahishi instead, and she keeps it hidden from both Pratapaditya and Vibha. When the Mahishi later shows the letter to Basanta Ray, he advises her not to reveal it to anyone else and to lie about its contents so that Vibha will not object to going to Chandradwip. Following his advice, the Mahishi tells Vibha and announces throughout the household that Ramchandra Ray has written a letter requesting that Vibha be sent to her in-laws' house.

Pratapaditya attempted to trap Ramchandra Ray by ordering the canal adjoining the royal palace, where Ramchandra’s boat was moored, to be blocked with large logs of Sal wood. Although the logs briefly stopped the escaping boat, Rammohan and his followers managed to pull the boat up and over the logs while the guards proved completely ineffective: the stones they threw failed to reach the boat, and since they only had swords, they wasted time frantically searching for a gun and then failing to find a flintlock, gunpowder, and bullets. Their subsequent attempt to pursue by boat also failed because the man sent to fetch a boat stopped on the way to smoke tobacco at Harimudi's shop and to wake Ramashankar to collect a debt; by the time the guards finished berating him for the delay, there was no longer any chance of catching Ramchandra's boat, which safely reached the Bhairav river.

When Basanta Ray is forced to part from Udayaditya because Udayaditya suffers on account of his love, his distress initially leads him to pick up his sitar and play it furiously with a great clatter. However, overcome by emotion and the sight of Vibha's tears, his eyes blur with tears and his throat becomes choked, hindering his playing until he is forced to stop and put the instrument down. Upon leaving, he abandons his sitar with Udayaditya, declaring that he will never play it again. Later in Raigarh, separated from Udayaditya and his loved ones, the sitar—once his "eternal companion"—is no longer with him as he dwells in emptiness and loses his joy in singing. When Khan Saheb notes that his music is no longer heard and asks about the sitar, Basanta Ray captures his deepening despair by stating that the sitar is still there, only its strings have broken and it can no longer be tuned.

Earlier, Udayaditya actively involved himself in the affairs of the subjects against Pratapaditya’s wishes, treated danger as a trifle, fought against oppression with all his might, and would stop officials to protect subjects without considering the consequences. After Surma’s death, however, a strange, blind fear of Pratapaditya overtakes him, causing him to lose his former courage and become consumed by hesitation and doubt in every matter. Consequently, he stops intervening to aid the oppressed: he cancels his plan to stop the looting and burning of the Chhapra zamindar's estate office, flees inside his house rather than rescuing a subject being beaten by a royal official, and lacks the courage to help Bhagavat and Sitaram financially—either openly or secretly—after their stipends are stopped.

After his conspiracy with Bhagavat leads to Udayaditya's imprisonment, Sitaram frees Udayaditya during the commotion of a fire that causes the guards to abandon their posts by throwing open his prison door, telling him the prison is on fire, grabbing and pulling him out of the prison, and leading him away to escape.

On the first occasion, to extract Ramchandra Ray from the royal palace of Jessore, Rammohan twists and ties thick sheets together to form a huge rope, ties it to a small pillar on the roof, and climbs down it with Ramchandra clinging to his back. At the end of the rope, he lets go with his hands, grips the rope with his teeth, releases Ramchandra from his back, lowers him carefully with both hands into the waiting boat below, and then jumps down himself, later helping his followers pull the boat up and over the large sal wood logs blocking the canal. On the second occasion, after Vibha faints and falls to the floor inside Ramchandra Ray's palace, Rammohan lifts her, brings her out of the palace, places her unconscious and exhausted body into one of the palanquins near the gate, and returns with her to the boat.

In Jessore, Vibha is heavily adorned by the Mahishi within the inner quarters, burdened with eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and a coiffure forced upon her by her mother. Despite being flustered by these ornaments, she presents a shy yet joyous face, struggling to keep her unruly glee from shining out. 

In Chandradwip, her attire and presentation undergo a stark reversal: stripped of royal status and pomp, she refuses a palanquin and steps out of the boat dressed as a common woman in a sari and veil, declaring she will go like a common subject or a beggar-woman. Pale, tear-filled, and moving through the crowds in a dazed, dreamlike state, she loses her usual shyness until a guard grabs her and her veil slips, leaving her mortified with shame. She enters the palace completely unwelcomed like any other maidservant and falls to the floor at Ramchandra Ray's feet, looking so diminished and unrecognizable that the king mistakes her for a beggar woman seeking alms.

In his bedchamber after Surma's death, the window symbolizes her absence, his grief, and a lingering flicker of hope of seeing her again, as he leaves her usual spot empty and gazes at the unchanged moonlight, garden, and breeze while hoping to find her sitting there whenever he enters the room. In the prison cell, the window transforms into a symbol of innate freedom and future liberation; looking through it at the sky and flying birds keeps away the surrounding darkness, reminds him that he is naturally free and cannot be held captive by any king or emperor, and gives him hope that his cage and the chains of his life will one day break.

Initially, the penniless Sitaram is drawn to both Rukmini’s beauty and her money, visiting her to borrow cash through witty rhymes and playful, flirtatious banter. Rukmini plays along by feigning affection, refusing to discuss interest, and encouraging him to call her affectionate names like "Pranpriye." As Sitaram stops repaying her and visits frequently, their relationship shifts into secret scheming together.

The dynamic turns hostile after Udayaditya (the Yubaraj) is imprisoned. Enraged, Sitaram storms into Rukmini’s house, curses her, nearly strikes her, and declares he is going to Raigarh to free the Yubaraj. He threatens to burn her house to ruins, grind her face on the stone floor, and drive her out of the city smeared with lime and soot. His outburst fills Rukmini with intense hatred and fierce possessiveness over Udayaditya, leaving her determined to thwart him.

The hostility escalates into a life-threatening encounter after Sitaram helps Udayaditya escape and stages a fire to fake his death. Believing Rukmini to be dead, Sitaram goes to her cottage late at night to steal her money before fleeing Jessore, only to find her sitting alive in the dim light, dripping wet and shivering. After recovering from thinking she is a ghost, Sitaram mocks her, prompting Rukmini to declare that she has returned from the door of Yama and will not die until she has destroyed both him and the Yubaraj and smeared herself with their funeral ashes. When Sitaram attempts to defuse the situation by reverting to his old tactic of feigning affection, Rukmini is consumed by fury. Finding no weapon within reach, she vows to make him pay and goes into the next room for a curved blade. Realizing his life is in genuine danger, Sitaram flees the cottage just before Rukmini returns with the blade and repeatedly strikes the floor where he had been standing.

Initially, Sitaram uses the fire as a distraction by having a few loyal commoners and palace servants simultaneously set five or six rooms of the guards' huts ablaze, which lures the guards away from Udayaditya's door and allows Sitaram to lead him out to escape. To prolong this chaos, Sitaram's men join the firefighting efforts and deliberately hinder them by pouring water where there is no fire, failing to return with water, breaking their water pots, and stumbling into one another. The strategy evolves into a cover-up to fake Udayaditya's death when Sitaram takes the Yubaraj's sword before disembarking from the escape boat and returns to the city. He takes back three letters Udayaditya had sent to the palace—keeping only those for the Mahishi and Vibha and destroying the third—while his men set fire to Udayaditya's empty prison cell. Finding the cell burning well, Sitaram throws bones, a skull, and Udayaditya's sword into the flames to plant evidence of his death. Finally, as men run to the guards fighting the guardhouse fire to report that the Yubaraj's cell is burning and that he was heard screaming inside, Sitaram runs up crying that the cell's roof has collapsed and there is no longer any response from Udayaditya, enabling him to spread the rumor that the Yubaraj perished in the fire rather than escaped.

Ramchandra Ray feels no gratitude toward Udayaditya, believing that being saved was simply bound to happen—and would have been wrong not to happen—since he assumes everyone would naturally unite to protect him in peril. He also believes that Udayaditya only rescued him for the sake of his own sister, and that saving Ramchandra's life was not Udayaditya's main objective. Disregarding Udayaditya's self-sacrifice, he treats him as guilty simply for being Pratapaditya's son and freely brings up his name to laugh, joke, and ridicule him alongside his courtiers.

Initially, Pratapaditya dismisses the minister's warnings about the Emperor of Delhi's anger and fifty thousand soldiers, though he immediately suspects Prince Udayaditya upon hearing that a complaint was lodged against him with the Emperor. Later, Bhagavat and Sitaram exploit this by forging a petition stamped with Udayaditya's seal, falsely portraying the prince as accusing Pratapaditya of treason to the Emperor of Delhi in order to obtain the kingdom for himself. Rather than taking the petition to Delhi, Bhagavat delivers it directly to Pratapaditya, claiming it was being carried toward Delhi by a servant of Udayaditya who has since fled. However, the provided context does not state that this resulted in Udayaditya's imprisonment; it only states that there is no need to describe Pratapaditya's state after reading the petition and that Bhagavat got his job back at the palace.

During Surma's presence in the palace, Vibha secretly goes to her to have her hair styled to her own liking when she finds the Mahishi's way of styling it unbearable, highlighting Surma's sympathetic care for her (even though the Mahishi assumes Surma ruined it out of jealousy and redoes it). After Surma is gone, when it is time to braid her hair, Vibha sits quietly waiting as if Surma will arrive at any moment to braid it for her; as evening gives way to night and Surma does not appear, Vibha's hair is left unbraided. Later, Vibha's hair remains unkempt, which Rammohan specifically notices alongside her sorrowful face as a sign that there is no longer anyone in the palace to care for her.
